title: Designing Composable, Least-Privilege Tools
summary: How you carve up tools decides whether an agent is reliable or chaotic. Small, single-purpose tools compose into behaviors the model can combine flexibly, while 'god-tools' that do everything through a mode flag confuse the model and concentrate risk. The pattern: give each tool one clear job, a predictable model-friendly signature, and the minimum permissions it needs — read-only where possible, narrow scope, no ambient authority — so the agent can chain tools safely and a single tool can never do more damage than its purpose requires.

subtopics.title: Single-purpose tools beat god-tools
subtopics.explanation: A god-tool like manage_user(action, ...) that branches on a string action is hard for the model to call correctly — it must guess which fields matter for which mode — and it concentrates every permission in one entry point. Splitting it into get_user, create_user, and deactivate_user gives the model unambiguous choices and lets you scope each one separately. Narrow tools are both easier for the model to select and safer to permission, which is why they compose better.
subtopics.example:
# god-tool: one entry point, ambiguous args, all permissions
def manage_user(action, user_id=None, email=None, role=None):
    if action == "get": ...
    elif action == "create": ...
    elif action == "deactivate": ...   # model must guess valid combos

# composable: one job each, individually scoped
def get_user(user_id: str) -> dict: ...          # read-only
def create_user(email: str, role: str) -> dict: ...  # write
def deactivate_user(user_id: str) -> dict: ...       # sensitive write
# the model picks exactly the capability it needs, nothing more

subtopics.title: Compose behaviors instead of configuring one tool
subtopics.explanation: With small tools, complex tasks emerge from the model chaining them — search_orders then get_order then issue_refund — rather than from one tool sprouting flags. Each tool's output feeds the next, and new behaviors come free from new combinations without touching existing tools. Composition is what lets a fixed toolset cover an open-ended range of tasks, which is the whole efficiency argument for the pattern.
subtopics.example:
# the agent composes narrow tools into a workflow it wasn't
# explicitly programmed for:
#   1. search_orders(customer="A. Rivera")   -> [order ids]
#   2. get_order(order_id="O-42")            -> {status, total}
#   3. issue_refund(order_id="O-42", amount=total)
#
# no single 'refund_customer_orders' god-tool needed; the model
# combines primitives, and each stays independently testable.
TOOLS = [search_orders, get_order, issue_refund]

subtopics.title: Scope each tool to least privilege
subtopics.explanation: Every tool should hold only the permissions its one job requires: a lookup tool gets a read-only, narrowly scoped credential; a write tool gets write only to its target; nothing gets ambient or admin authority. Because the model can be manipulated (prompt injection) into calling any exposed tool, the blast radius of a bad call is capped by whatever that tool was allowed to do. Least privilege is the control that turns a compromised step into a contained one rather than a breach.

subtopics.title: Give tools predictable, model-friendly signatures
subtopics.explanation: The model calls a tool by reading its name, description, and parameter schema, so a good signature is explicit and self-describing: a verb-noun name, required fields typed and constrained (enums, ranges), no overloaded 'options' blob, and a description that states exactly when to use it. Ambiguous or overloaded signatures cause the model to omit fields or misuse the tool. Predictable signatures are what make the model's tool calls correct on the first try, cutting retries and errors.

subtopics.title: Make tools predictable and side-effect-honest
subtopics.explanation: A tool should do exactly what its name and description promise and no more — get_order must not also log the user out, and a tool named read_file must never write. Hidden side effects make the model's plans wrong, because it reasons from the declared purpose. Keeping tools honest and idempotent where possible is what lets the model (and you) trust that a chain of calls has only the effects it appears to have.
subtopics.example:
# DISHONEST: name says read, but it mutates state
def read_config(key):
    audit_log.append(key)         # ok-ish
    cache.clear()                 # surprise side effect! plans break
    return CONFIG[key]

# HONEST + idempotent: read means read; effects match the name
def read_config(key: str) -> str:
    return CONFIG[key]            # no hidden mutation

def clear_cache() -> None:        # side effect gets its OWN named tool
    cache.clear()
# the model reasons correctly because names tell the truth

foundations.overview: Tool design is agent design. The decisive choice is granularity: many small, single-purpose tools versus a few 'god-tools' that multiplex behavior through a mode flag and a bag of optional arguments. Small tools win on two axes at once. For the model, a narrow tool with a clear verb-noun name, typed and constrained parameters, and an honest description is easy to select and call correctly, so it composes primitives (search then fetch then act) into open-ended workflows without you programming each one. For security, each narrow tool can be handed only the permissions its single job needs — read-only credentials for lookups, tightly scoped write for mutations, no ambient authority — so that when the model is manipulated into a bad call (prompt injection is always possible), the blast radius is capped by that one tool's least-privilege scope. Two supporting rules complete the pattern: signatures must be predictable and model-friendly (no overloaded options blobs), and tools must be side-effect-honest so the name and description tell the whole truth about what a call does. Together these produce agents that are both more capable (via composition) and safer (via containment).
foundations.formalDefinition: The composable least-privilege tool pattern prescribes decomposing agent capabilities into single-responsibility tools, each with (a) a predictable, self-describing signature (verb-noun name, typed/constrained required parameters, no mode-flag overloading), (b) permissions scoped to exactly that tool's function (least privilege, no ambient authority), and (c) honest, ideally idempotent semantics matching its description, such that complex tasks arise from the model composing tools while any single tool's failure or hijack is contained.
foundations.whyItMatters: Because a model can always be steered into calling any tool you expose — via ambiguous instructions or prompt injection — the permission scope of each tool is the real security boundary of an agent, and its clarity is the real reliability boundary. God-tools maximize both risk (one over-privileged entry point) and error (ambiguous calls); composable least-privilege tools minimize both while covering more tasks, which is why this pattern underlies every production-grade agent toolset.
foundations.mentalModel: Design tools like Unix commands: each does one thing well, has a clear name and typed flags, reads or writes but is honest about which, and you pipe them together for power. You would never ship a single `do_everything --mode=...` binary running as root; you ship `ls`, `cat`, `rm`, each with the least privilege it needs, and let composition provide the flexibility.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Support agents built from search_orders / get_order / issue_refund with per-tool credential scopes and refund caps; coding agents with separate read_file / write_file / run_tests where write and execute are the guarded tools; internal agents where sensitive mutations are split out as individually approved, tightly scoped tools rather than folded into a broad admin action.
commonUseCases: Splitting a god-tool into scoped single-purpose tools
Separating read, write, and destructive actions into distinct tools

commonMisconceptions.myth: Fewer tools is simpler and therefore better.
commonMisconceptions.reality: One god-tool is simpler to list but harder for the model to call correctly and impossible to scope tightly; several narrow tools are easier to select and each is independently permissioned and testable.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Least privilege doesn't matter because the model is 'aligned'.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The model can be manipulated (prompt injection) into calling any exposed tool. Only the tool's own permission scope caps the damage, so least privilege is the actual boundary.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Extra parameters and modes make a tool more flexible.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Overloaded signatures make the model omit or misuse fields and hide side effects. Flexibility should come from composing small honest tools, not from configuring one.

interactiveExamples.title: Refactor a god-tool into composable tools
interactiveExamples.explanation: Take a manage_order(action, ...) god-tool and split it into three single-purpose tools. Notice the narrow tools have unambiguous signatures the model can call correctly and can be permissioned separately, while the god-tool forces the model to guess valid action/field combinations.

code.caption: Each narrow tool has a required, typed signature and one job — easy for the model to pick and simple to scope, unlike the flag-driven god-tool.

interactiveExamples.title: Enforce least privilege at the tool boundary
interactiveExamples.explanation: Wrap each tool so it can only exercise the permissions its purpose needs, and prove the containment: a read tool cannot write, and a refund tool caps the amount and requires approval above a threshold. This is what limits the blast radius when the model is steered into a bad call.

code.caption: Scopes are the security boundary: the read-only tool physically cannot refund, and even the refund tool caps auto-approval, so a manipulated call stays contained.

checkpoints.prompt: Why do single-purpose tools compose better than a god-tool with an 'action' flag?
options: They give the model unambiguous choices and can each be scoped/permissioned separately
checkpoints.explanation: Narrow tools are easy for the model to select and call correctly, and each can hold only the permissions its one job needs — so behaviors compose while risk stays contained per tool.

checkpoints.prompt: The model can be prompt-injected into calling any tool you expose. What most limits the damage of a bad call?
options: The least-privilege scope of the specific tool that was called
checkpoints.explanation: Since any exposed tool can be triggered, each tool's own permission scope is the real security boundary. A read-only or narrowly scoped tool caps the blast radius regardless of why it was called.

checkpoints.prompt: This tool is 'read-only' by name but violates the pattern. What's wrong?
checkpoints.code:
def read_user(user_id: str) -> dict:
    user = db.get(user_id)
    db.touch_last_seen(user_id)   # writes!
    audit.wipe_old()              # deletes!
    return user
options: A tool named read_user has hidden write and delete side effects, so the model's plans and the least-privilege scope are both wrong
checkpoints.explanation: The tool is side-effect-dishonest: its name promises a read but it mutates and deletes. That breaks the model's reasoning and means it needs far broader privileges than a read tool should. Split the effects into their own named tools.

theory.question: Why are many small single-purpose tools generally preferable to a few multi-purpose 'god-tools' in an agent?
theory.directAnswer: Because narrow tools are both easier for the model to use and safer to permission. A single-purpose tool has an unambiguous name and typed signature the model can call correctly, composes with others into open-ended workflows, and can be scoped to exactly the privileges its one job needs — so a hijacked or buggy call is contained. God-tools multiplex behavior through a mode flag, making the model guess valid argument combinations and concentrating every permission in one over-broad entry point.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A granularity principle: decompose capabilities into single-responsibility tools rather than one configurable multi-action tool.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Models select tools by reading names/descriptions/schemas, and can be manipulated into calling any exposed tool; both reliability and security therefore depend on clarity and per-tool scoping.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Give each tool one job, a verb-noun name, typed constrained parameters, and only the credentials it needs; complex tasks then emerge from the model chaining primitives, while each tool's least-privilege scope caps its blast radius.

theory.whyImportant: Tool granularity is simultaneously the reliability boundary (clear calls, fewer retries) and the security boundary (contained blast radius) of an agent, so it is one of the highest-leverage design decisions.
theory.realWorldExample: Splitting manage_order(action,...) into get_order (read-only), refund_order (capped write), and cancel_order lets the model compose a refund flow correctly while a compromised lookup can never issue a refund.

followUps.question: Doesn't more tools overwhelm the model's context?
followUps.answer: Very large toolsets can, so you group by task and expose only relevant tools per step (or via MCP servers), but you still favor narrow tools over god-tools within that set.

followUps.question: When is a slightly broader tool acceptable?
followUps.answer: When the sub-actions share the same permission scope and the model reliably fills the arguments; the line is drawn where scoping or clarity would suffer.

theory.question: What does 'least privilege' mean for agent tools, and why is it the real security boundary?
theory.directAnswer: Least privilege means each tool holds only the permissions its single function requires — read-only credentials for lookups, tightly scoped write for mutations, no ambient or admin authority, short-lived tokens. It is the real boundary because the model can be manipulated (via ambiguous instructions or prompt injection) into calling any tool you expose, so you cannot rely on the model 'choosing well'; the only hard cap on damage is what the invoked tool was permitted to do.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The practice of scoping every tool's credentials and capabilities to the minimum needed for its purpose.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Because tool selection is model-controlled and manipulable, permission scope — not model behavior — is what actually contains a bad call.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Mint per-tool credentials scoped to the exact resource and action, prefer read-only, add caps/approvals on sensitive writes, use short TTLs, and deny ambient network/filesystem access so a hijacked tool cannot exceed its declared job.

theory.whyImportant: It converts an inevitable class of failures (the model being steered into a wrong call) from a potential breach into a contained, low-impact event, which is what makes autonomous tool use safe to run.
theory.realWorldExample: A read-only get_order tool given only 'orders:read' physically cannot issue a refund even if a prompt-injected message tells the agent to; the refund tool separately caps auto-approval and escalates larger amounts.

followUps.question: How does least privilege interact with prompt injection?
followUps.answer: It's the containment layer: injection may cause a bad tool call, but a tightly scoped tool bounds what that call can accomplish, turning a breach into a contained error.

followUps.question: What about destructive actions like delete?
followUps.answer: Split them into their own narrowly scoped tools with confirmation/approval gates, never fold them into a broader tool where they'd inherit wide access.

scenario.question: You inherit a support agent exposing one admin_action(action, target, payload) tool holding a full-admin token. It works but occasionally takes wrong actions and is a security worry. How do you redesign the toolset?
scenario.directAnswer: Decompose admin_action into single-purpose tools (get_ticket, reply_ticket, issue_refund, deactivate_account, ...), give each a credential scoped to exactly its function, and gate destructive ones behind caps and human approval. Fix signatures to be typed and constrained so the model calls them correctly, make each side-effect-honest, and expose only the tools a given flow needs. Roll out behind evaluation on real transcripts to confirm the model composes the narrow tools correctly.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A refactor from a single over-privileged god-tool to a composable least-privilege toolset.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The god-tool causes both failure modes at once: ambiguous action/payload combos make the model act wrongly, and one full-admin token means any wrong (or injected) call can do anything.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Enumerate the distinct actions, create one tool per action with a typed schema and its own minimal scope, add caps/approval to sensitive writes, remove the broad token, then A/B the new toolset against saved conversations to verify correct composition and no regressions before full rollout.

scenario.whyImportant: It demonstrates fixing reliability and security together through granularity and scoping rather than patching prompts, which is the durable fix for over-broad agent tools.
scenario.realWorldExample: After splitting the tool and scoping tokens, a later prompt-injection attempt could at most trigger a capped refund that required approval, instead of the full-admin deactivate-and-refund the old tool allowed.

followUps.question: How do you avoid overwhelming the model with the new, larger toolset?
followUps.answer: Expose tools by task/flow (or via separate MCP servers) so only relevant ones are in context at each step, keeping selection accurate.

followUps.question: How do you validate the refactor didn't regress behavior?
followUps.answer: Replay saved transcripts through both toolsets and compare outcomes, plus add evals for the sensitive flows (refunds, deactivations) before rollout.

keyTakeaways: Prefer many small single-purpose tools over god-tools: they give the model unambiguous choices and can each be scoped and tested independently.
Get power from composition — the model chains narrow primitives (search then fetch then act) — not from adding modes and flags to one tool.
Scope every tool to least privilege; since the model can be prompt-injected into any call, a tool's permission scope is the real security boundary that caps blast radius.
Design predictable, model-friendly signatures: verb-noun names, typed/constrained required fields, no catch-all options blob, and a description stating when to use it.
Keep tools side-effect-honest and idempotent where possible so names tell the truth, letting the model (and you) reason correctly about a chain of calls.
